author: reek
body: The format solver. A DeckGenome is an archetype: a color, a land / creature / spell split, and an AI Personality. genome-to-deck realises it as a real 60-card deck from the bridged pool. A gauntlet plays every genome against every other and tallies wins, surfacing the deck that survives the field. Genomes mutate between generations, so the field co-evolves toward stronger decks. This is the skeleton of "output the deck that survives a rigorous test" -- one generation is a round-robin; evolve-genomes advances the field.

author: reek
body: A genome whose splash colour differs from its main colour is a two-colour deck: mostly its main colour, with a handful of off-colour "answer" spells (a blue control deck splashing white for Wrath of God and Swords to Plowshares is the classic). The splash is supported by dual lands that make both colours, a few splash-colour basics, and the any-colour rocks the deck already runs (Black Lotus, Fellwar Stone). When splash equals the main colour the deck is mono and takes the unchanged build path.

author: reek
body: Play one game between two genomes; return the winner (0 = a, 1 = b, -1 = draw / turn limit).

author: reek
body: Total wins for one genome across games against every other genome. Each ordered pair is played once, so with N genomes each plays 2*(N-1) games (on the play and on the draw, different seeds).

author: reek
body: The rigorous gauntlet scores each genome by total match wins over R best-of-three matches against every opponent -- R times the sample of the plain gauntlet, so the standings reflect deck strength rather than a single lucky pairing. Callers pass repeats; repeats = 1 reduces to the plain gauntlet.

author: reek
body: A survivor is one answer; the richer answer is the whole matchup grid -- which deck beats which, and by how much. matchup-matrix plays every ordered pair over R best-of-three matches and records each cell as a win percentage (a deck against itself is skipped, marked -1). From the grid, field-winrates gives each deck its average win rate across the field; best-index names the top deck; and meta-spread (best average minus worst) measures format health -- a tight spread is a balanced format, a wide one is warped toward a dominant deck.

author: reek
body: A genome is viable against a pool only when the pool holds at least one creature of its color. With none, build-color-deck cycles an empty list and the deck is all lands -- it cannot win, so leaving it in the gauntlet would silently skew every score (a real risk on artifact-heavy sets like Antiquities). viable-field drops such genomes; callers report the drop rather than fielding a dead deck.

author: reek
body: Mutate a genome's ratios and personality toward variation. Lands stay in a sane band; creatures and spells shift by a small delta that keeps the 60-card total. The personality mutates via the existing GA.

author: reek
body: The splash colour is part of the genome the GA explores. Roughly a third of mutations reroll it to a random colour -- which may land back on the main colour (dropping the splash to mono) or on a new second colour (adding or changing a splash). Over generations the gauntlet selects for splashes that actually help, rather than the splash being a fixed hand-picked choice. A rerolled splash into a colour the pool cannot support just yields a slightly weaker deck the gauntlet selects against, so no guard is needed here (build-splash-deck still returns a legal 60-card deck when the splash has no spells).

author: reek
body: genome-breed crosses the parts the gauntlet can judge and holds the parts that identify the archetype. Name and main colour come from the first parent, because the main colour picks the card pool and a crossed colour would field a deck whose name disagrees with its spells; genome-viable already refuses a colour the pool cannot support, and crossover there would just manufacture those. Lands, the creature/spell split, the splash colour, the sideboard budget and the Personality all cross. The 60-card total is preserved the same way mutate-genome preserves it: creatures are clamped into the band the chosen land count leaves, and spells take the remainder.

author: reek
body: The consequence to know: a child carries its first parent's name, exactly as a mutated genome does, so an evolved field can hold two genomes with one name and different ratios. A name alone therefore stops identifying a deck once crossover is in play, and any report that names the survivor has to print its ratios beside the name.
